title: Plant Systematics - Sept 2026
description: A comprehensive review of nomenclature, land plants, diagnostic plant families, phylogenetics, molecular data, tree support, and Exam 1 applications.

lessons.title: Taxonomy, systematics, and characters
lessons.body: Taxonomy describes, identifies, names, and classifies organisms. Plant systematics includes all of taxonomy and reconstructs evolutionary history with phylogenies. A character is an observable biological variable, such as petal shape, stamen number, or a nucleotide position; a character state is its particular expression, such as ovate, five, or G.
lessons.definition: The study of plant diversity that combines taxonomy with reconstruction of evolutionary relationships.
lessons.memoryTip: Taxonomy organizes and names; systematics also explains ancestry.

lessons.title: Scientific names and the ICN
lessons.body: A species name contains an italicized Genus plus lowercase specific epithet, followed by a non-italicized authority. The genus is capitalized. The authority first validly published the species. After transfer to another genus, the original authority goes in parentheses and the transferring authority follows. The ICN requires a physical type specimen, publication in primary peer-reviewed literature, and a formal English or Latin description.

image.alt: Annotated scientific plant name showing a capitalized genus, lowercase specific epithet, and non-italicized authority.
image.caption: Scientific-name anatomy from the source lecture PDF

lessons.definition: The two-part Genus plus specific-epithet naming system designed by Linnaeus; the authority is an additional, non-italicized attribution.
lessons.memoryTip: Quercus alba L.: capital Genus, lowercase epithet, plain-text authority.

lessons.title: Rank, position, and classification
lessons.body: Rank is a categorical level: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum or Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Position is a taxon's particular placement inside the higher groups. Members of one family share an order but do not have to share a genus. Classification is derived from hypotheses of evolutionary history, so it can change as phylogenies improve; named taxa should be monophyletic.
lessons.definition: A taxon's specific placement within higher-ranking taxonomic groups.
lessons.memoryTip: Rank is the level; position is the address at that level.

lessons.title: Land plants
lessons.body: Land plants evolved from a shared green-algal ancestor. Their terrestrial adaptations include a waxy cuticle that limits water loss and protected multicellular embryos. The major groups are bryophytes, lycophytes, monilophytes (ferns and allies), gymnosperms, and angiosperms. Red algae may be informally called plants because many are photosynthetic and multicellular, but their chloroplast lineage has an origin independent from the green-plant lineage, most are aquatic, and they lack embryophyte land adaptations. Plant groups are defined by shared characteristics.
lessons.definition: Land plants, distinguished in part by retaining and protecting multicellular embryos.
lessons.memoryTip: Cuticle keeps water in; the parent plant keeps the embryo protected.

lessons.title: Asteraceae structure
lessons.body: A head or capitulum is a specialized inflorescence that resembles one flower but contains many small florets attached to a common receptacle. The involucre and its phyllaries form the base around the head. The pappus is a calyx modified into hairs, bristles, scales, or awns atop the ovary or achene and often aids dispersal. Asteraceae is a large family with many fall-blooming species.

image.alt: Botanical diagram labeling the capitulum, receptacle, involucre, phyllaries, pappus, and major Asteraceae floret forms.
image.caption: Asteraceae morphology from the source lecture PDF

lessons.definition: A composite flower head of many florets attached to a shared receptacle.
lessons.memoryTip: One apparent flower is a community of florets.

lessons.title: Asteraceae florets and heads
lessons.body: Ray florets have one strap-like petal ending in three lobes or teeth. Disk florets have a tube of fused petals ending in five small lobes. Ligulate florets are strap-shaped and end in five lobes. Radiate heads combine central disk florets with an outer ring of rays; discoid heads contain only disk florets; ligulate heads contain only ligulate florets, as in dandelions. Daisies, sunflowers, and Solidago are radiate examples in the guide.

image.alt: Three photographed Asteraceae flower heads labeled radiate, discoid, and ligulate.
image.caption: Asteraceae head types from the source lecture PDF

lessons.definition: A head with central disk florets surrounded by an outer ring of ray florets.
lessons.memoryTip: Ray = strap with 3 teeth; ligulate = strap with 5; disk = tube with 5.

lessons.title: The graminoid families
lessons.body: Graminoid is an informal morphology term for grasses, sedges, and rushes: plants with tiny flowers and long, thin leaves that can dominate habitats. Poaceae have round hollow jointed stems, open sheaths with a ligule, spikelets with feathery stigmas and dangling stamens, and caryopsis fruits. Cyperaceae have solid triangular stems, three-ranked leaves with closed sheaths, spikelets without a perianth, and achenes. Juncaceae have round solid stems, basal or three-ranked leaves, flowers with six chaffy tepals and three stamens, and round capsules.
lessons.definition: An informal descriptor for grass-like monocots, not a formal family name.
lessons.memoryTip: Reeds have joints, sedges have edges, and rushes are round.

lessons.title: Reading phylogenetic trees
lessons.body: A lineage is an ancestor-descendant sequence of populations through time. A node is a split or speciation event and represents the most recent common ancestor of its descendant clades. An internode is the branch between successive nodes. The root or base is the deepest ancestral lineage; tips are modern terminal taxa. Shared branches and nodes indicate shared common ancestry, and a phylogeny is a testable hypothesis of relationships and character evolution.

image.alt: Rooted tree of tomato, fern, sponge, mouse, and mushroom with internal nodes labeled a through e.
image.caption: Practice tree embedded in the Exam 1 Word document

lessons.definition: A branching point representing a common ancestor and lineage-splitting event.
lessons.memoryTip: Root is oldest, nodes are splits, internodes connect splits, tips are terminals.

lessons.title: Clades and character evolution
lessons.body: A monophyletic group or clade contains a common ancestor and every descendant. A paraphyletic group omits one or more descendants; a polyphyletic group combines descendants from separate ancestors. A plesiomorphic state is ancestral. An apomorphy is derived; a synapomorphy is shared and derived and unites multiple taxa, while an autapomorphy is derived and unique to one terminal taxon.
lessons.definition: A shared, derived homologous character state that supports a clade of two or more taxa.
lessons.memoryTip: Mono = all descendants; para = some; poly = separate origins.

lessons.title: Homology, homoplasy, and reticulation
lessons.body: Homology is similarity inherited from a common ancestor. Homoplasy is similarity not caused by common descent. It can arise by convergence—independent evolution under comparable pressures—or reversal to an ancestral state. An outgroup lies outside the ingroup and roots the tree so ancestral and derived states can be distinguished. Standard cladograms bifurcate, but hybridization merges lineages and produces network-like reticulation.
lessons.definition: Similarity caused by convergence or reversal rather than direct shared ancestry.
lessons.memoryTip: Homology shares history; homoplasy only shares appearance or state.

lessons.title: Mapping and molecular characters
lessons.body: Use the outgroup's states as ancestral and map transitions to derived states. Parsimony favors the fewest state changes, including necessary convergence or reversal. Branch length may be proportional to evolutionary changes, often base substitutions, and is interpreted with a scale bar. In aligned DNA, each nucleotide position is a character with A, C, T, or G states; invariant sites are uninformative. An indel is an insertion or deletion.

image.alt: Four candidate trees labeled a through d mapping transitions among character states zero, one, and two.
image.caption: Character-history exercise embedded in the Exam 1 Word document

lessons.definition: Preference for the explanation or tree requiring the smallest number of evolutionary transitions.
lessons.memoryTip: Polarize with the outgroup, then count the fewest changes.

lessons.title: DNA regions and tree construction
lessons.body: Chloroplast loci such as rbcL, matK, and ndhF are usually maternally inherited in angiosperms, non-recombining, and slower, making them useful at family or order depth. Nuclear DNA such as ITS is biparentally inherited and faster, useful for recent species relationships and hybridization. Angiosperms353 targets 353 single-copy nuclear protein-coding genes across deep and shallow clades. Maximum parsimony minimizes steps; maximum likelihood chooses the topology most likely under a substitution model; Bayesian analysis uses MCMC posterior probabilities; ASTRAL reconciles gene trees under the coalescent and handles incomplete lineage sorting.
lessons.definition: A universal target-capture panel for 353 single-copy nuclear protein-coding genes.
lessons.memoryTip: Parsimony counts steps, likelihood models substitutions, Bayesian samples posteriors, ASTRAL combines gene trees.

lessons.title: Branch lengths, support, and consensus
lessons.body: Cladogram branch lengths are arbitrary and show topology only; phylogram lengths measure divergence as changes or substitutions per site. Parsimony and likelihood bootstrap support resamples alignment columns with replacement; over 70% is good. Bayesian posterior probability is strong above 0.90. In ASTRAL, a supporting-gene proportion over 0.5 is acceptable, while below 0.5 is weak. A polytomy has more than two immediate descendants and may reflect uncertainty, insufficient data, or rapid divergence. A strict consensus of equally parsimonious trees keeps clades present in every tree and collapses conflicts into polytomies.
lessons.definition: A summary retaining only clades found in 100% of candidate trees and collapsing conflicts.

lessons.title: Applying phylogenetic evidence
lessons.body: To compare relatedness, find the most recent common ancestor: two taxa are equally related to a third when their pairwise comparisons lead to the same ancestral node. In a character-by-taxon matrix, compare states column by column. A shared derived state supports a proposed clade, while a conflicting state may imply another relationship or homoplasy. Published trees should be read together with their stated data, reconstruction method, branch-length meaning, and support values. If a named genus is not monophyletic, classification can be revised by splitting it into monophyletic genera or expanding it to include the omitted descendants.

image.alt: Published orchid phylogeny showing species assigned to Coelogyne in two separated groups and related genera between them.
image.caption: Classification-revision example embedded in the Exam 1 Word document

lessons.definition: A change in taxon boundaries or names intended to make classification reflect a supported phylogenetic hypothesis.
lessons.memoryTip: Locate the ancestor, compare each character, check support, then make every named group a clade.

questions.prompt: How does plant systematics differ from taxonomy?
questions.answer: Taxonomy describes, identifies, names, and classifies plants; systematics also reconstructs evolutionary history with phylogenies.
acceptedAnswers: systematics includes taxonomy and reconstructs evolutionary history
taxonomy names and classifies while systematics also studies phylogeny
questions.hint: One discipline includes the other and adds evolutionary relationships.
questions.explanation: Plant systematics encompasses taxonomy and also reconstructs evolutionary history using phylogenetics.

questions.prompt: In a dataset where petal shape is recorded as linear or ovate, what are “petal shape” and “ovate,” respectively?
options: Character and character state
Character state and character
Rank and position
Taxon and authority
questions.answer: Character and character state
acceptedAnswers: character and character state
questions.hint: The variable comes first; its particular expression comes second.
questions.explanation: A character is the observable variable, while a character state is its particular condition.

questions.prompt: Using the figure, which formatting of the illustrated species name is correct?

questions.prompt: How are authorities shown when a species is transferred to a different genus?
questions.answer: Put the original describing authority in parentheses, followed by the transferring authority outside the parentheses.
acceptedAnswers: original authority in parentheses followed by the transferring authority
the original author is parenthesized and the revising author follows
questions.hint: Distinguish the original author from the author who made the new combination.
questions.explanation: Reclassification preserves the original authority in parentheses and places the transferring authority after it.

questions.prompt: What three requirements in the study guide must be met to formally name a species under the ICN?
questions.answer: Designate a physical type specimen, publish in primary peer-reviewed scientific literature, and provide a formal English or Latin description.
acceptedAnswers: physical type specimen peer reviewed publication and english or latin description
questions.hint: Think specimen, publication, and description.
questions.explanation: The guide lists a physical type, primary peer-reviewed publication, and a formal description in English or Latin.

questions.prompt: Distinguish taxonomic rank from taxonomic position, and state what taxa in the same family must share.
questions.answer: Rank is the hierarchical category, position is placement within higher groups, and members of one family share the same order but not necessarily the same genus.
acceptedAnswers: rank is category position is placement and the same family shares an order
questions.hint: Rank is a level; position is an address. Look one level above family.
questions.explanation: Rank names the category, position locates the taxon, and a family's taxa share an order but may occupy different genera.

questions.prompt: Why is biological classification subject to change?
options: It is derived from evolving phylogenetic hypotheses
Authorities expire after a century
Ranks are chosen randomly
The ICN prohibits stable names
questions.answer: It is derived from evolving phylogenetic hypotheses
acceptedAnswers: it is derived from evolving phylogenetic hypotheses
questions.hint: Classification should reflect evolutionary history.
questions.explanation: New evidence can change phylogenetic hypotheses and therefore the classifications derived from them.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches the study guide's foundations of classification?
options: Linnaeus designed the naming system, and plant groups are defined by shared characteristics
Darwin designed binomial nomenclature, and groups are defined only by habitat
Authorities determine groups by publication date alone
Plant groups cannot change after they are named
questions.answer: Linnaeus designed the naming system, and plant groups are defined by shared characteristics
acceptedAnswers: linnaeus designed the naming system and plant groups are defined by shared characteristics
questions.hint: Recall the historical name in the guide and the evidence used to recognize groups.
questions.explanation: The guide credits Linnaeus with the naming system and emphasizes that shared characteristics define plant groups.

questions.prompt: Name the shared ancestor and two defining terrestrial adaptations of land plants.
questions.answer: Land plants share a green-algal ancestor and have a waxy cuticle plus protected multicellular embryos.
acceptedAnswers: green algal ancestor waxy cuticle and protected multicellular embryos
questions.hint: One adaptation reduces water loss; the other protects developing offspring.
questions.explanation: Embryophytes arose from a green-algal ancestor and are adapted with a cuticle and protected multicellular embryos.

questions.prompt: List the five major land-plant groups in the study guide and explain why red algae are excluded.
questions.answer: Bryophytes, lycophytes, monilophytes, gymnosperms, and angiosperms; red algae lack embryophyte land adaptations.
acceptedAnswers: bryophytes lycophytes monilophytes gymnosperms angiosperms and red algae lack land plant adaptations
questions.hint: Move from bryophytes through flowering plants, then contrast Archaeplastida red algae.
questions.explanation: Those five are the major embryophyte groups; red algae are Archaeplastida but lack embryophyte terrestrial adaptations.

questions.prompt: What is an Asteraceae capitulum, and where are its florets attached?
questions.answer: It is a specialized inflorescence that mimics one flower but contains many florets attached to a common receptacle.
acceptedAnswers: many florets attached to a common receptacle
a composite head of florets on one receptacle
questions.hint: The apparent single flower is actually a head of tiny flowers.
questions.explanation: The capitulum is a specialized composite inflorescence of many florets on a shared receptacle.

questions.prompt: In the source diagram, which pairing correctly identifies a radiate head and a discoid head?

options: Radiate: disk plus ray florets; discoid: disk florets only
Radiate: ligulate florets only; discoid: ray florets only
Radiate: disk florets only; discoid: disk plus ray florets
Both contain ligulate florets only
questions.answer: Radiate: disk plus ray florets; discoid: disk florets only
acceptedAnswers: radiate disk plus ray florets discoid disk florets only
questions.hint: Look at whether an outer ray is present.
questions.explanation: Radiate heads combine central disks and outer rays, while discoid heads consist exclusively of disks.

questions.prompt: Define the pappus and the involucre or phyllaries in an Asteraceae head.
questions.answer: The pappus is a modified calyx of hairs, bristles, scales, or awns that can aid dispersal; phyllaries collectively form the involucre around the base of the head.
acceptedAnswers: pappus is modified calyx for dispersal and phyllaries form the involucre
questions.hint: One is the fluffy or spiky calyx; the other wraps the head's base.
questions.explanation: The pappus is the modified calyx atop the ovary or achene, while phyllaries make up the basal involucre.

questions.prompt: Compare ray, disk, and ligulate florets by shape and number of terminal lobes or teeth.
questions.answer: A ray floret is strap-shaped with three teeth, a disk floret is tubular with five lobes, and a ligulate floret is strap-shaped with five teeth.
acceptedAnswers: ray strap three disk tube five ligulate strap five
questions.hint: Two are straps but have different tooth counts; one is a tube.
questions.explanation: Rays are 3-toothed straps, disks are 5-lobed tubes, and ligulates are 5-toothed straps.

Daisy: ligulate; left pink: radiate; center pink: discoid

questions.prompt: Which statement about “graminoid” is correct?
options: It is an informal descriptor for grass-like monocots
It is the formal family containing all grasses and sedges
It means any plant with a hollow stem
It is a phylogenetic rank above order
questions.answer: It is an informal descriptor for grass-like monocots
acceptedAnswers: it is an informal descriptor for grass-like monocots
questions.hint: The word is lowercase in the guide for a reason.
questions.explanation: Graminoid describes the shared grass-like form of Poaceae, Cyperaceae, and Juncaceae; it is not a formal taxon.

questions.prompt: Which ecological and seasonal summary appears in the study guide?
options: Asteraceae is large with many fall bloomers, and graminoids can be important habitat species
Asteraceae contains only spring bloomers, and graminoids are ecologically minor
Graminoids have broad leaves and large flowers
Asteraceae contains only a few species
questions.answer: Asteraceae is large with many fall bloomers, and graminoids can be important habitat species
acceptedAnswers: asteraceae is large with many fall bloomers and graminoids can be important habitat species
questions.hint: Recall the key-point summary immediately before the graminoid table.
questions.explanation: The guide notes both the abundance of fall-blooming Asteraceae and the importance of graminoids in some habitats.

questions.prompt: Give the stem, sheath, inflorescence, and fruit traits that diagnose Poaceae in the guide.
questions.answer: Round hollow jointed stems, open sheaths with a ligule, spikelets with feathery stigmas and dangling stamens, and a caryopsis or grain.
acceptedAnswers: round hollow jointed stem open sheath ligule spikelets feathery stigmas dangling stamens caryopsis
questions.hint: “Reeds have joints”; then recall the open sheath, ligule, spikelets, and grain.
questions.explanation: That complete trait combination distinguishes the grass family in the study guide.

questions.prompt: Give the stem, leaf or sheath, flower, and fruit traits that diagnose Cyperaceae.
questions.answer: Solid triangular stems, three-ranked leaves with closed sheaths, tiny flowers in spikelets without a perianth, and achene fruits.
acceptedAnswers: solid triangular stems three ranked leaves closed sheaths spikelets no perianth achenes
questions.hint: “Sedges have edges,” closed sheaths, and no perianth.
questions.explanation: Cyperaceae combine edged solid stems, three-ranked closed-sheath leaves, perianth-less spikelets, and achenes.

questions.prompt: Give the stem, leaf, flower, and fruit traits that diagnose Juncaceae.
questions.answer: Round solid stems, basal or three-ranked leaves, tiny flowers with six chaffy tepals and three stamens, and round capsules.
acceptedAnswers: round solid stems basal or three ranked leaves six chaffy tepals three stamens round capsules
questions.hint: “Rushes are round,” including the solid stem and capsule.
questions.explanation: The rush family has round solid stems and capsules plus regular flowers with six chaffy tepals and three stamens.

questions.prompt: Define lineage, node, internode, root, and tip on a phylogenetic tree.
questions.answer: A lineage is an ancestor-descendant sequence; a node is a split and common ancestor; an internode joins successive nodes; the root is the deepest ancestor; tips are terminal taxa.
acceptedAnswers: lineage ancestor descendant sequence node split common ancestor internode between nodes root deepest ancestor tips terminal taxa
questions.hint: Describe the path, split, connector, oldest base, and living or sampled ends.
questions.explanation: These five terms describe the paths and landmarks used to interpret tree topology.

questions.prompt: Contrast monophyletic, paraphyletic, and polyphyletic groups, and state which form named taxa should take.
questions.answer: Monophyletic includes an ancestor and all descendants and is the form named taxa should take; paraphyletic includes the ancestor but only some descendants; polyphyletic combines lineages from separate ancestors.
acceptedAnswers: monophyletic all descendants named taxa paraphyletic some descendants polyphyletic separate ancestors
questions.hint: Focus on whether all, some, or separately originated descendants are included.
questions.explanation: Only a monophyletic clade contains one ancestor and every descendant; named taxa should ideally have this form.

questions.prompt: Distinguish plesiomorphy, apomorphy, synapomorphy, and autapomorphy.
questions.answer: A plesiomorphy is ancestral, an apomorphy is derived, a synapomorphy is shared and derived, and an autapomorphy is derived and unique to one terminal taxon.
acceptedAnswers: plesiomorphy ancestral apomorphy derived synapomorphy shared derived autapomorphy unique derived
questions.hint: Start with ancestral versus derived, then ask whether a derived state is shared or unique.
questions.explanation: These terms distinguish ancestral states from derived states and whether a derived state diagnoses a clade or one tip.

questions.prompt: What does a phylogeny represent, and what do shared branches and nodes mean?
options: A hypothesis of relationships and character evolution; shared branches and nodes indicate common ancestry
A permanent classification; shared branches indicate identical habitats
A list of names; nodes indicate taxonomic rank
A geographic map; branches indicate distance
questions.answer: A hypothesis of relationships and character evolution; shared branches and nodes indicate common ancestry
acceptedAnswers: a hypothesis of relationships and character evolution shared branches and nodes indicate common ancestry
questions.hint: Trees are testable explanations, not permanent facts.
questions.explanation: Phylogenies hypothesize relatedness and trait history, with shared tree structure representing shared ancestors.

questions.prompt: Contrast homology and homoplasy, and name the two processes that produce homoplasy in the guide.
questions.answer: Homology is similarity from common ancestry; homoplasy is similarity not from common descent and can result from convergence or reversal, which may not always be distinguishable.
acceptedAnswers: homology common ancestry homoplasy not common ancestry convergence reversal
questions.hint: One reflects shared history; the other can arise independently or return to an old state.
questions.explanation: Convergence independently creates similar states; reversal returns a lineage to an ancestral state. Both are homoplasy and may sometimes be difficult to distinguish.

questions.prompt: What does an outgroup do, and why does hybridization violate a purely bifurcating tree model?
questions.answer: An outgroup roots the tree and identifies ancestral versus derived states; hybridization merges lineages and creates reticulate, network-like evolution.
acceptedAnswers: outgroup roots tree polarizes characters hybridization merges lineages reticulation
questions.hint: One provides direction; the other reconnects branches.
questions.explanation: The external outgroup polarizes change, while hybridization joins branches that a simple splitting diagram keeps separate.

questions.prompt: Describe the parsimony procedure for mapping characters onto a tree.
questions.answer: Treat outgroup states as ancestral, map transitions to derived states, and choose the mapping with the fewest total changes while allowing convergence or reversal when necessary.
acceptedAnswers: outgroup ancestral map derived transitions fewest changes convergence reversal
questions.hint: First polarize states, then apply Occam's razor.
questions.explanation: Parsimony maps the minimum number of state transitions after the outgroup establishes polarity.

questions.prompt: When a tree's branch lengths are meaningful, what may they represent in this study guide?
options: Evolutionary changes, often base substitutions, interpreted with a scale bar
The physical height of each plant
Only the number of sampled taxa
Taxonomic rank
questions.answer: Evolutionary changes, often base substitutions, interpreted with a scale bar
acceptedAnswers: evolutionary changes often base substitutions interpreted with a scale bar
questions.hint: The scale might be a number of changes or substitutions per base pair.
questions.explanation: Meaningful branch lengths can be proportional to evolutionary change and require the scale bar for interpretation.

questions.prompt: How are aligned nucleotide sites used as characters, and why are invariant sites uninformative? Define an indel too.
questions.answer: Each aligned position is a character whose states are A, C, T, or G; a site shared by every taxon cannot distinguish relationships; an indel is an insertion or deletion.
acceptedAnswers: aligned position character a c t g invariant sites cannot distinguish taxa indel insertion or deletion
requiredConcepts: a c t g|adenine cytosine thymine guanine
questions.hint: Variation among taxa supplies phylogenetic information; also expand the word indel.
questions.explanation: Nucleotide positions are characters, bases are states, invariant columns lack grouping information, and indel abbreviates insertion/deletion.

questions.prompt: Compare chloroplast DNA and nuclear DNA for inheritance, evolutionary rate, and best phylogenetic depth; give examples.
questions.answer: Chloroplast rbcL, matK, and ndhF are usually maternal, non-recombining, slower, and useful for family or order depth; nuclear ITS is biparental, faster, and useful for recent species relationships and hybridization.
acceptedAnswers: chloroplast maternal non recombining slow deep rbcL matK ndhF nuclear biparental fast shallow ITS hybridization
questions.hint: Contrast organelle versus nuclear inheritance and deep versus shallow resolution.
questions.explanation: The slower chloroplast markers fit deeper splits, whereas faster biparental nuclear ITS resolves recent relationships and reticulation.

questions.prompt: What is Angiosperms353?
options: A universal target-capture panel for 353 single-copy nuclear protein-coding genes
A chloroplast with 353 base pairs
